chunks: "W/L is the width-to-length ratio of the transistor's channel.
The length is the distance between source and drain that the carriers travel, and the width is how wide the channel is, so you can think of the transistor as many parallel strips of channel.
A wider channel carries more current, and a longer channel resists it more, so the drive strength scales with W/L.
In the equations it's inside k equals micro C oxW over L : the saturation current is 1 over 2 k(V GS-V t) squared , the transconductance is k V ov , and the on-resistance is about 1 over (k V ov) .
Double W/L and you double the current and gm and halve R on .
The catch is that gate capacitance goes up with the gate area, W times L , so a bigger W costs more input capacitance, which slows whatever drives it and increases dynamic power.
In a CMOS inverter that's the trade: wider devices switch the load faster but present more load to the previous stage.
You also typically make the PMOS about 2 to 3 times wider than the NMOS to compensate for hole mobility. Length is chosen separately. Minimum L gives the speed in digital logic.
In analog, you use longer L for higher output resistance and better matching.
And in power MOSFETs, a huge effective W/L, from millions of parallel cells, is how you get milliohms."
